opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because in some sense they're two answers to the same question: how do you get a system that writes code to get better at writing code over time, using what it's seen before?

DreamCoder makes that explicit. You solve some problems, you look at the programs you found, you pull out the reusable pieces, and you add them to a library as new primitives. Then you train a neural network to guide search over programs written in that growing language. The appeal is that the knowledge is symbolic and inspectable. You can open the library and see that it has invented something like `map` or `fold`, or some domain-specific concept for drawing or for physics equations. And because it's compressed into a small set of abstractions, it generalizes in a fairly systematic way.

A large language model trained on code does something that looks similar, but it's implicit and on a vastly larger scale. It has absorbed huge numbers of human-written libraries and idioms, so in a sense it starts with a library far richer than anything DreamCoder could learn from scratch on a few hundred tasks. That's a big practical win. DreamCoder was bottlenecked on search. Discovering useful abstractions from very little data is hard, and the wake-sleep loop is expensive. Foundation models mostly bypass that bootstrapping problem.

What you give up is the explicitness. With a foundation model you don't know exactly what abstractions it has, you can't easily edit them, and it's not obvious how it should accumulate new ones for a domain it hasn't seen. If you put a model in front of a new family of problems, it doesn't naturally write down "here's the concept I just learned, let me reuse it next time." It might do in-context learning, but that's transient.

So I don't see them as competitors so much as complementary. The direction I find most exciting is using the language model as the prior and the proposal mechanism, the thing that makes search tractable, while keeping something like an explicit, growing library on top. The model writes candidate programs, and you refactor what works into reusable functions, maybe with the model's help naming and documenting them. Then those functions get fed back in as context or tools for the next round of problems. You get the broad human prior from pretraining, plus the continual, compositional, inspectable learning that DreamCoder was going for.

And I think that last part, learning that accumulates and stays legible, still matters a lot. Humans don't just pattern-match against everything they've seen. We build up concepts, name them, and compose them. That's partly what makes our knowledge transferable and communicable. Library learning is one way of getting machines to do a bit more of that, and foundation models finally make it practical to try at a scale where it could matter.

r001.rationale: The response describes foundation models as implicitly drawing on code, libraries, and idioms learned from prior examples, in a way similar to DreamCoder’s explicit library learning.

r002.rationale: The response cites search bottlenecks, difficulty discovering abstractions, and the cost of the wake-sleep loop, but does not identify automatically debugging an entire program library as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly calls the approaches complementary and proposes combining a foundation model’s prior with a growing explicit library.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because in some sense the big models have eaten part of what DreamCoder was trying to do, and in another sense they've made the core problem more interesting rather than less.

The way DreamCoder worked, you have a wake phase where you're trying to solve problems by searching for programs, and then a sleep phase where you look back at the solutions you found and ask, what are the recurring pieces here? And you compress them out into a library. So the library is this very explicit, inspectable artifact. You can open it up and see, oh, it discovered map, it discovered fold, it discovered this notion of a repeated structure in a drawing. And then the neural network is trained to recognize when those library pieces are likely to be useful, so the search gets faster on the next round. The knowledge lives in two places, the symbolic library and the weights of the recognition model, and they're coupled.

Now with a large language model, you don't have to build the library from scratch. The model already knows what fold is, it knows every idiom in every language on GitHub. So the question becomes, what's the equivalent of library learning when the prior is already that strong? And I think the honest answer is that a lot of it moves into the context window. When you put past solved examples in the prompt, you're doing something that's functionally very similar to what the library was doing. You're saying, here are abstractions that worked on related problems, reuse them. Retrieval over past programs is a kind of soft, implicit library.

But I don't think that means the explicit version is dead. There are a few things the explicit library gives you that in-context examples don't. One is compression. DreamCoder's library is small, it's a handful of functions, and when you refactor your solutions in terms of them the programs get much shorter, which means search gets exponentially cheaper. If you're just stuffing a hundred past solutions into a prompt, you don't get that. You're paying linearly for every example and the model has to figure out on the fly what's shared. The other thing is that the explicit library is a form of understanding you can actually look at. When the system discovers a new concept, you can name it, you can check whether it's right, you can hand it to a human. With a foundation model doing everything in-weights or in-context, that concept might be there but it's diffuse.

So where I've landed, and this is roughly the direction my group has been going, is that you want both. Use the foundation model as the proposal distribution, because it's an incredibly good prior over programs, far better than anything we could train from scratch in 2020. But keep the outer loop. Keep the idea that you solve some problems, you look at what you solved, you consolidate it into reusable pieces, and you feed that back in, either as new functions the model can call, or as fine-tuning data, or just as a curated set of examples. The sleep phase is still doing real work, it's just that the thing it's refining is a much more capable model.

And I'd actually argue the wake-sleep framing matters more now, not less. Because a frozen foundation model is fixed. It doesn't get better at your domain just because you've used it a thousand times. If you want a system that becomes an expert in some narrow area over time, whether that's a weird DSL, or a scientific modeling language nobody wrote much code in, you need some mechanism for turning experience into durable knowledge. Library learning was one answer to that. I think the modern answer looks a lot like it, with the symbolic parts and the neural parts rebalanced.

r001.rationale: The response says past solved examples in a prompt function like DreamCoder’s library and calls retrieval over past programs a “soft, implicit library.”

r002.rationale: The response does not identify automatic debugging of an entire program library as an obstacle to constructing reusable libraries.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly argues to use both: foundation models as proposal distributions while retaining the outer loop that consolidates solutions into reusable pieces.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. In DreamCoder, the idea is that you solve a collection of tasks, look at the programs you’ve written, and identify reusable pieces. You turn those pieces into functions, add them to your library, and then use that library to make solving future tasks easier. So there’s an explicit representation of what you’ve learned: you can inspect it, execute it, and compose it with other things.

A large language model can also learn patterns from programs, but much of that knowledge lives implicitly in its weights. It might generate code that uses a common pattern without ever turning that pattern into a named abstraction. And that’s a very powerful way to transfer knowledge, but it’s a different mechanism from building a library.

What interests me is combining them. You could use a foundation model to propose solutions, then use execution and tests to check them, and look across the successful solutions for abstractions worth retaining. Those abstractions could then become tools available to the model on subsequent tasks.

The tricky part is deciding what deserves to become an abstraction. Compressing the programs you’ve already seen is one signal, but ultimately you want a library that helps you solve new problems. A useful abstraction doesn’t just save you a few lines of code; it makes the next problem easier to express and easier to search for a solution to.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models learn program patterns implicitly in their weights, but describes this as a different mechanism from building a library. It does not characterize code generation from successful examples as an implicit form of DreamCoder’s library learning.

r002.rationale: The response mentions checking proposed solutions with execution and tests, but does not identify the difficulty of automatically debugging an entire program library as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly calls the approaches complementary, contrasting DreamCoder’s inspectable, reusable library with foundation models’ implicit learned patterns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary ways of exploiting experience. With DreamCoder, we make that experience explicit: you solve a collection of tasks, look for structure shared across the solutions, and turn that structure into reusable functions. Those functions then change the language in which you solve the next set of tasks. So you’re learning both how to search and what building blocks to search over.

A large language model can absorb patterns from past programs into its weights and use those patterns to generate new programs. That’s an enormously powerful way to guide search, but it doesn’t necessarily give you an explicit library that you can inspect, execute, and compose.

The distinction isn’t absolute, though. A foundation model can propose abstractions, and it can write code that uses a learned library. You could imagine using the model to generate candidate solutions, testing those solutions, and then looking across the successful programs for abstractions worth keeping. Those abstractions could become tools available to the model on subsequent tasks.

For me, the interesting question is how to close that loop: how does solving problems improve the representations and tools you use to solve future problems? Library learning gives you a very concrete mechanism for doing that, and foundation models give you a very powerful source of proposals.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models absorb patterns from past programs into their weights, but does not characterize this as an implicit form of DreamCoder’s library learning.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the difficulty of automatically debugging a library of programs.

r003.rationale: It explicitly presents DreamCoder’s explicit library learning and foundation models’ implicit pattern learning as complementary ways to exploit experience.
